screens.title: Storing and Loading Game Data with Save Games
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model of Unreal Engine's SaveGame system and why it matters to player experience. Persisting progress, settings, inventory and world flags keeps players engaged across sessions and prevents frustration. We'll define the core components: a custom SaveGame Blueprint that holds variables, the GameplayStatics nodes that write and read slots, and the practical pattern of populating a SaveGame object before saving and applying its values after loading. You'll see a compact workflow you can reuse: create a SaveGame object, populate it with the player's current data, then call the save node with a slot name and user index. We will also cover safety checks like Does Save Game Exist and how to handle missing slots gracefully. A concrete example we'll work toward is saving player health and location from a ThirdPersonCharacter on a key press and restoring them when the game starts or when you press load. By the end of this chapter you will understand serialization and deserialization in UE, how to structure SaveGame Blueprints, and common pitfalls so your saves remain reliable. Think about one game state you must preserve in your project — how would you represent that inside a SaveGame Blueprint?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Overview
Storing and Loading Game Data with Save Games
Design reliable persistence using SaveGame Blueprints and GameplayStatics nodes for saving to and loading from disk.
In this lesson
Create SaveGame classes, save player state to slots, and restore state safely on load.
Why it matters
Persistence keeps player progress intact between sessions and allows features like multiple slots and auto-save.
Practical demo goal
Save player health and location from the character on key press; load it back and restore the actor state on demand.
Explore Key Topics
SaveGame Blueprint
A container class that holds the variables serialized to disk.
GameplayStatics
Nodes used to create, save, check, and load save files by slot name.
Slot Management
Use slot names and user index to manage multiple save files and players.
Visual concept
SaveGame object acts as a snapshot. Populate variables, then write to disk with a slot name; later load, cast, and apply.
Quick pattern
Create SaveGame Object → Set variables → Save Game to Slot. For load: Does Save Game Exist → Load Game from Slot → Cast → Apply values.
Common mistake: forgetting to set SaveGame variables before Save Game to Slot. That saves empty state.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In these learning objectives we make clear, measurable outcomes you can aim for as you work through the SaveGame system. First, you will be able to explain the purpose and architecture of Unreal's SaveGame system: why a custom SaveGame Blueprint exists, what it serializes, and how the GameplayStatics nodes read and write slots. Second, you'll create a basic SaveGame Blueprint and define variables like player health, location, and arrays that will be persisted. Defining variables in the SaveGame Blueprint, not only in the player or game mode, is important because only those declared on the SaveGame class are serialized automatically. Third, you'll implement logic to save player progress at runtime: create the SaveGame object, populate it with current values, and call Save Game to Slot with a slot name and user index. Fourth, you'll implement reliable load logic that checks for the slot, loads the SaveGame object, casts to your class, and applies saved values back to active actors. Each objective focuses on both the technique and why it prevents lost progress or corrupted state.

screens.title: Practical Skills and Scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on scenarios and operational skills you'll practice. You will implement save/load triggers from gameplay events such as checkpoints, quitting, or explicit key presses. Learn to manage multiple slots and automatic saves by constructing slot names dynamically — for example prefixing with SaveSlot_ or AutoSave — and using a user index to separate local players. You will also learn to separate settings persistence from player progress by using distinct SaveGame Blueprints, such as one for game settings and another for player progress. Crucially, you will practice handling actor state that cannot be saved by reference. Instead of saving actor pointers, record identifiers and the minimal state needed to restore behavior — for instance a door's unique name and its open boolean. Finally, you will learn common validation patterns: check Does Save Game Exist before loading, handle None returns after Load Game from Slot, and initialize default saves when needed. These steps keep your game robust across first-run and corrupted-save scenarios.

screens.title: What is a SaveGame Blueprint?
screens.narratorSegment: A SaveGame Blueprint is a custom class that inherits from Unreal's USaveGame and acts as the blueprint for your save file. In practical terms it is a container where you declare the variables you want written to disk. These variables are automatically serialized when you call the save node and deserialized when you load. The key design point is that only variables declared inside a SaveGame Blueprint — or in custom Structs and Enums referenced by it — are included in the serialized snapshot. Variables that live in PlayerController, GameMode, or arbitrary Actors are not saved automatically. For example, if you want to persist player health and location, you add a float and a vector variable to BP_PlayerSaveGame. If you need to track an inventory, include an array of item structs in the SaveGame. A common misconception is attempting to save direct actor references; actor pointers are not serialized for you. Instead, record identifiers or state primitives and rebind them on load. Remember: the SaveGame Blueprint defines the shape of the data written to disk; designing that shape thoughtfully is the first step toward reliable persistence. What would you include in your game's primary SaveGame container and why?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › SaveGame Blueprint
SaveGame Blueprint: definition
A serializable container class used to declare the exact variables written to disk.
What to store
Primitives and custom structs: health, location, arrays of item structs, quest names, and simple booleans for actor state.
What not to store
Direct actor references and runtime-only pointers — instead save identifiers and state values to re-establish references on load.
Design tip
Keep the SaveGame focused: avoid storing large transient caches. Store the minimal authoritative data needed to restore the game state.
Concrete example
A BP_PlayerSaveGame with variables: SavedPlayerName (String), SavedHealth (Float), SavedLocation (Vector), InventoryItems (Array of Structs).
Analogy
Think of the SaveGame Blueprint as the form template you fill out each time you take a snapshot of the game state.
Key Takeaway

Declare every variable you want persisted inside the SaveGame Blueprint. Design structs for complex data and avoid storing actor references directly.

screens.title: Save workflow: create, populate, save
screens.narratorSegment: Saving is a predictable sequence of actions. First, create an instance of your SaveGame Blueprint using the Create SaveGame Object node and specify your BP class. This yields an empty SaveGame object. Second, populate that object: read values from the player or game state — current health, actor locations, inventory contents — and set the corresponding variables on the SaveGame object. This step is crucial: saving an unpopulated object is a common source of bugs. Third, call Save Game to Slot with the SaveGame object, a slot name string like PlayerSlot or AutoSave, and a user index integer for local players. A concrete example: on pressing the Save key, your ThirdPersonCharacter calls Create SaveGame Object for BP_MyPlayerSaveGame, casts the result to that class, sets SavedHealth to the character's Health, sets SavedLocation to GetActorLocation, assigns a SavedPlayerName, and then calls Save Game to Slot with slot name "PlayerSlot" and user index 0. Common misconceptions include believing Save Game to Slot updates existing files without repopulating the object; instead always set the current values on the SaveGame instance before saving. After calling the save node, provide player feedback such as a small notification to confirm persistence. How will you ensure your Save trigger always gathers fresh state before writing?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Save Workflow
Save workflow
Create → Populate → Save
1. Create SaveGame Object
Instantiate BP_PlayerSaveGame using Create SaveGame Object.
2. Populate variables
Set SavedHealth, SavedLocation, inventory arrays and other fields from current game state.
3. Save Game to Slot
Call Save Game to Slot with the filled SaveGame object, slot name string, and user index.
Key Takeaway

Always populate the SaveGame object with current values before invoking Save Game to Slot. Use explicit slot names and user index for clarity.

Concrete scenario
Save on key press: Create SaveGame Object, cast to BP_MyPlayerSaveGame, Set SavedHealth = Health, Set SavedLocation = GetActorLocation, Save Game to Slot "PlayerSlot", User Index 0.
Common mistake
Saving without setting variables will write an empty snapshot. Always set fields on the SaveGame object instance first.

screens.title: Load workflow: check, load, cast, apply
screens.narratorSegment: Loading is the mirror of saving but requires cautious checks. The safe pattern begins with Does Save Game Exist using the intended slot name and user index. If it returns false, treat this as a first-run scenario and initialize defaults or create a SaveGame object. If it exists, call Load Game from Slot with the same slot name and user index. Load Game from Slot returns a generic SaveGame object; you must cast it to your specific SaveGame Blueprint to access the saved variables. Once cast, read values like SavedHealth and SavedLocation and apply them to your active actors: set the player's Health variable, teleport the character to SavedLocation, and restore inventory arrays. A common misconception is assuming Load Game from Slot will always succeed — always guard against None and handle failures gracefully. Also avoid applying loaded values blindly to all objects; validate that the receiving actor is present and in a valid state. For example, loading a door state requires finding the door by the saved name, then setting its IsOpen boolean. End your load routine with small feedback like a printed message or UI toast to confirm success. What default state will you initialize when no save exists for your project?

Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Load Workflow
Load workflow
Does Save Game Exist → Load Game → Cast → Apply
1. Does Save Game Exist
Check for a save file before attempting to load to avoid None returns.
2. Load Game from Slot
Load the generic SaveGame object from disk using the same slot name and user index.
3. Cast and apply
Cast to your BP class, then set Health, Teleport player, and apply inventory contents with validation.
Key Takeaway

Always guard loads with existence checks and casting. Validate actors before applying saved state to avoid runtime errors.

Concrete scenario
On game start: if Does Save Game Exist returns true, Load Game from Slot, cast to BP_PlayerSaveGame, set player Health and Set Actor Location to SavedLocation. If false, initialize defaults like full health and spawn at start location.
Misconception
Assuming Load Game from Slot always returns your custom class. It returns a generic SaveGame; you must cast to access custom variables.

screens.title: Slot Names and User Index
screens.narratorSegment: Slot names and the user index together form the identifier for a save file on disk. The slot name is a string — for example "PlayerSlot", "SaveSlot_0", or "AutoSave" — that you choose to organize files. The user index is an integer used to disambiguate saves for different local players on the same machine; in single-player projects you typically use zero. Choosing clear, consistent slot naming conventions is a small design decision with large operational impact: it makes loading straightforward and prevents accidental overwrites. Compare two strategies: a single slot approach uses one consistent name for autosaves; a multiple-slot approach builds slot names dynamically to support manual save slots or per-level saves. If you want three manual slots, generate names like SaveSlot_0, SaveSlot_1, SaveSlot_2. A common misconception is relying on implicit defaults for user index — always set it explicitly when calling save/load nodes. Another pitfall is reusing a slot name unconsciously and overwriting a player's important progress. Concrete advice: adopt a naming pattern up front and centralize slot name generation in a small utility function or blueprint to avoid inconsistent usage. Which slot strategy best fits your game's save UX and why?

keyIdea.text: Use clear slot names and an explicit user index. Decide between single auto-save slots and multiple manual slots based on your game's UX needs.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Slot Strategy
Slot Names vs. User Index
Organize saves with consistent naming and explicit user indices.
Single-slot (auto-save)
Use one slot like "AutoSave" for periodic autosaves. Simple but risk overwriting progress if user expects multiple slots.
Multiple slots (manual saves)
Generate names like SaveSlot_0, SaveSlot_1 to let players choose where to save. Requires UI to select and manage slots.
User index
Use user index to separate local player saves. For single-player projects, use 0 consistently to avoid ambiguity.
Naming best practice
Centralize slot name creation in a small utility to avoid typos and accidental overwrites across blueprints.

screens.title: Handling actor state and references
screens.narratorSegment: One of the trickiest aspects of persistence is world actor state. Actors live in memory and their runtime references cannot be serialized directly in a portable way. The recommended pattern is to store an actor's unique identifier and the minimal state required to restore it. For example, to preserve whether a door is open, save its unique name and an IsOpen boolean. On load, locate the actor by that name or stored ID, then set its state accordingly. If you need richer actor snapshots, design small Structs that contain the actor's identifier and only the necessary fields to reconstruct behavior. Avoid saving entire actor components or references; instead save lightweight representations and reconstruct runtime links after loading. A common misconception is trying to persist complex object graphs by reference. That will not reliably serialize and will often produce broken references on load. A practical restoration step: after loading, iterate saved actor entries, find matching actors in the level, and apply saved booleans and transforms. If an actor is missing, you may spawn a default instance or skip gracefully. How will you identify persistent actors in your level to rebind them on load?

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › Actor State
Actor state persistence
Persist identifiers and minimal fields, then rebind actors on load.
Save format
Create structs with ActorName (string) and state fields like IsOpen boolean or CurrentHealth.
Restore routine
After loading, for each saved actor entry find actor by name and set its properties. If not found, handle gracefully.
Design tradeoffs
Choosing the minimal set of fields reduces save size and simplifies restoration logic.
Example
To save a door: store DoorName (string) and IsOpen (bool). On load: Find Actor by DoorName and call SetIsOpen(IsOpen).
Common mistake
Attempting to save Actor references directly. Those references won't be meaningful after restarting the level or the editor.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.3 › ThirdPersonCharacter Save/Load
Blueprint pseudocode
// Input Action Save (Pressed)
Create SaveGame Object (SaveGame Class: BP_MyPlayerSaveGame)
→ Cast To BP_MyPlayerSaveGame (As SaveRef)
  → Set SaveRef.SavedHealth = Self.Health
  → Set SaveRef.SavedLocation = Self.GetActorLocation()
  → Set SaveRef.SavedPlayerName = "Hero"
  → Save Game to Slot (SaveRef, "PlayerSlot", 0)
  → Print String "Game Saved!"

// Input Action Load (Pressed)
Does Save Game Exist ("PlayerSlot", 0)
→ Branch (If True)
  → Load Game from Slot ("PlayerSlot", 0)
  → Cast To BP_MyPlayerSaveGame (As LoadedRef)
    → Self.Health = LoadedRef.SavedHealth
    → Set Actor Location (Self, LoadedRef.SavedLocation, Teleport: True)
    → Print String "Game Loaded!"
→ Branch (If False)
  → Print String "No Save Game Found!"
Example test plan
Place player in level, take damage or move, press Save, then change position or damage, press Load and confirm health and position revert to saved values.
Pro Tip
Use descriptive saved player names in the SaveGame to help debug which save file is loaded during tests.
Key Takeaway

Follow the exact sequence: create, populate, save; check existence, load, cast, apply. Test by saving and restoring to confirm persistence.

screens.title: Serialization and Deserialization
screens.narratorSegment: Serialization is the process of converting variables declared in a SaveGame Blueprint into a storable format on disk. Deserialization is the reverse: reading that stored data and restoring values into a SaveGame object at runtime. In Unreal, declaring variables on a SaveGame Blueprint signals the engine that those fields should be included in the save snapshot. Structs and enums defined in Blueprints are also serializable if referenced by the SaveGame. Serialization does not include runtime references, transient pointers, or ephemeral engine state that isn't represented as saved fields. A practical example: a SavedLocation vector is serialized and later deserialized into a vector value you can use to set actor transforms. A misconception is thinking that private transient variables or values stored only in local function scope are automatically saved — they are not. To ensure correct serialization, define everything you need as a variable on the SaveGame or in a serializable struct. Lab: Save and Load Health & Location
A short checklist to produce a working save system in your character blueprint.

screens.title: Troubleshooting and validation
screens.narratorSegment: During implementation you will likely run into a few recurring issues. First, saving before populating the SaveGame object results in empty or default data on disk. Remedy: always set fields on the SaveGame instance every time you save. Second, using inconsistent slot names or user indices leads to loading the wrong file or failing to find a save. Remedy: centralize slot name generation and pass the same values to save and load nodes. Third, attempting to save actor references leads to invalid references after restarting the level. Instead store identifiers and restore by searching for the actor on load. Another issue is failing to handle Does Save Game Exist returning false. If your code assumes a save exists, Load Game from Slot will return None and your cast will fail. Always check existence before loading and provide a default initialization path for new players. For debugging, print or log the SaveGame fields immediately after creating and populating the object to verify contents before calling Save Game to Slot. A final tip: separate settings saves from progress saves so changing one does not overwrite the other. After you fix these patterns, your save system will be far more robust. What validation checks will you add to your save and load routines to catch errors early?

Fix common mistakes that break saves or loads.
Forgot to populate
Always set SaveGame fields before calling Save Game to Slot. Verify by printing values before saving.
Wrong slot name or index
Centralize slot generation to avoid typos and mismatched names between save and load.
No existence check

Actor references
Save actor identifiers instead of direct references, then rebind on load.

Use separate SaveGame BPs for settings and progress to avoid accidental overwrites.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model of Unreal Engine's SaveGame system and why it matters to player experience. Persisting progress, settings, inventory and world flags keeps players engaged across sessions and prevents frustration. We'll define the core components: a custom SaveGame Blueprint that holds variables, the GameplayStatics nodes that write and read slots, and the practical pattern of populating a SaveGame object before saving and applying its values after loading. You'll see a compact workflow you can reuse: create a SaveGame object, populate it with the player's current data, then call the save node with a slot name and user index. We will also cover safety checks like Does Save Game Exist and how to handle missing slots gracefully. A concrete example we'll work toward is saving player health and location from a ThirdPersonCharacter on a key press and restoring them when the game starts or when you press load. By the end of this chapter you will understand serialization and deserialization in UE, how to structure SaveGame Blueprints, and common pitfalls so your saves remain reliable. Think about one game state you must preserve in your project — how would you represent that inside a SaveGame Blueprint?

In these learning objectives we make clear, measurable outcomes you can aim for as you work through the SaveGame system. First, you will be able to explain the purpose and architecture of Unreal's SaveGame system: why a custom SaveGame Blueprint exists, what it serializes, and how the GameplayStatics nodes read and write slots. Second, you'll create a basic SaveGame Blueprint and define variables like player health, location, and arrays that will be persisted. Defining variables in the SaveGame Blueprint, not only in the player or game mode, is important because only those declared on the SaveGame class are serialized automatically. Third, you'll implement logic to save player progress at runtime: create the SaveGame object, populate it with current values, and call Save Game to Slot with a slot name and user index. Fourth, you'll implement reliable load logic that checks for the slot, loads the SaveGame object, casts to your class, and applies saved values back to active actors. Each objective focuses on both the technique and why it prevents lost progress or corrupted state.

These objectives focus on scenarios and operational skills you'll practice. You will implement save/load triggers from gameplay events such as checkpoints, quitting, or explicit key presses. Learn to manage multiple slots and automatic saves by constructing slot names dynamically — for example prefixing with SaveSlot_ or AutoSave — and using a user index to separate local players. You will also learn to separate settings persistence from player progress by using distinct SaveGame Blueprints, such as one for game settings and another for player progress. Crucially, you will practice handling actor state that cannot be saved by reference. Instead of saving actor pointers, record identifiers and the minimal state needed to restore behavior — for instance a door's unique name and its open boolean. Finally, you will learn common validation patterns: check Does Save Game Exist before loading, handle None returns after Load Game from Slot, and initialize default saves when needed. These steps keep your game robust across first-run and corrupted-save scenarios.

A SaveGame Blueprint is a custom class that inherits from Unreal's USaveGame and acts as the blueprint for your save file. In practical terms it is a container where you declare the variables you want written to disk. These variables are automatically serialized when you call the save node and deserialized when you load. The key design point is that only variables declared inside a SaveGame Blueprint — or in custom Structs and Enums referenced by it — are included in the serialized snapshot. Variables that live in PlayerController, GameMode, or arbitrary Actors are not saved automatically. For example, if you want to persist player health and location, you add a float and a vector variable to BP_PlayerSaveGame. If you need to track an inventory, include an array of item structs in the SaveGame. A common misconception is attempting to save direct actor references; actor pointers are not serialized for you. Instead, record identifiers or state primitives and rebind them on load. Remember: the SaveGame Blueprint defines the shape of the data written to disk; designing that shape thoughtfully is the first step toward reliable persistence. What would you include in your game's primary SaveGame container and why?

Saving is a predictable sequence of actions. First, create an instance of your SaveGame Blueprint using the Create SaveGame Object node and specify your BP class. This yields an empty SaveGame object. Second, populate that object: read values from the player or game state — current health, actor locations, inventory contents — and set the corresponding variables on the SaveGame object. This step is crucial: saving an unpopulated object is a common source of bugs. Third, call Save Game to Slot with the SaveGame object, a slot name string like PlayerSlot or AutoSave, and a user index integer for local players. A concrete example: on pressing the Save key, your ThirdPersonCharacter calls Create SaveGame Object for BP_MyPlayerSaveGame, casts the result to that class, sets SavedHealth to the character's Health, sets SavedLocation to GetActorLocation, assigns a SavedPlayerName, and then calls Save Game to Slot with slot name "PlayerSlot" and user index 0. Common misconceptions include believing Save Game to Slot updates existing files without repopulating the object; instead always set the current values on the SaveGame instance before saving. After calling the save node, provide player feedback such as a small notification to confirm persistence. How will you ensure your Save trigger always gathers fresh state before writing?

Loading is the mirror of saving but requires cautious checks. The safe pattern begins with Does Save Game Exist using the intended slot name and user index. If it returns false, treat this as a first-run scenario and initialize defaults or create a SaveGame object. If it exists, call Load Game from Slot with the same slot name and user index. Load Game from Slot returns a generic SaveGame object; you must cast it to your specific SaveGame Blueprint to access the saved variables. Once cast, read values like SavedHealth and SavedLocation and apply them to your active actors: set the player's Health variable, teleport the character to SavedLocation, and restore inventory arrays. A common misconception is assuming Load Game from Slot will always succeed — always guard against None and handle failures gracefully. Also avoid applying loaded values blindly to all objects; validate that the receiving actor is present and in a valid state. For example, loading a door state requires finding the door by the saved name, then setting its IsOpen boolean. End your load routine with small feedback like a printed message or UI toast to confirm success. What default state will you initialize when no save exists for your project?

Slot names and the user index together form the identifier for a save file on disk. The slot name is a string — for example "PlayerSlot", "SaveSlot_0", or "AutoSave" — that you choose to organize files. The user index is an integer used to disambiguate saves for different local players on the same machine; in single-player projects you typically use zero. Choosing clear, consistent slot naming conventions is a small design decision with large operational impact: it makes loading straightforward and prevents accidental overwrites. Compare two strategies: a single slot approach uses one consistent name for autosaves; a multiple-slot approach builds slot names dynamically to support manual save slots or per-level saves. If you want three manual slots, generate names like SaveSlot_0, SaveSlot_1, SaveSlot_2. A common misconception is relying on implicit defaults for user index — always set it explicitly when calling save/load nodes. Another pitfall is reusing a slot name unconsciously and overwriting a player's important progress. Concrete advice: adopt a naming pattern up front and centralize slot name generation in a small utility function or blueprint to avoid inconsistent usage. Which slot strategy best fits your game's save UX and why?

One of the trickiest aspects of persistence is world actor state. Actors live in memory and their runtime references cannot be serialized directly in a portable way. The recommended pattern is to store an actor's unique identifier and the minimal state required to restore it. For example, to preserve whether a door is open, save its unique name and an IsOpen boolean. On load, locate the actor by that name or stored ID, then set its state accordingly. If you need richer actor snapshots, design small Structs that contain the actor's identifier and only the necessary fields to reconstruct behavior. Avoid saving entire actor components or references; instead save lightweight representations and reconstruct runtime links after loading. A common misconception is trying to persist complex object graphs by reference. That will not reliably serialize and will often produce broken references on load. A practical restoration step: after loading, iterate saved actor entries, find matching actors in the level, and apply saved booleans and transforms. If an actor is missing, you may spawn a default instance or skip gracefully. How will you identify persistent actors in your level to rebind them on load?
